lessons.title: Lab: Memory and connection sizing

scenes.text: A server with 32 GB RAM and max_connections = 1000 swaps under load.
Size memory sensibly and put PgBouncer in front.

steps.title: Starting points
steps.body:
- `shared_buffers` ≈ 25% of RAM
- `effective_cache_size` ≈ 50–75% of RAM (planner hint)
- `work_mem` is **per sort/hash operation per connection** — keep modest
- Use a pooler (PgBouncer) instead of thousands of backends

steps.title: Risk maths
steps.body: 100 connections × 4 sorts × 64 MB work_mem = 25.6 GB potential.

steps.title: Mistakes
steps.body:
- Huge max_connections
- Huge work_mem globally (set per role/session for reports instead)

lessons.title: Lab: Roles, privileges and least privilege

steps.body: Users and groups are both **roles**. Pattern: `orders_owner` (owns schema, NOLOGIN), `orders_app` (LOGIN, DML only), `orders_ro` (SELECT only), humans in groups.

steps.title: Mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES (new tables not granted)
- Granting on PUBLIC schema in PG < 15 defaults

lessons.title: Lab: Ticket — 'permission denied for table invoices'

scenes.text: Finance reports fail after the weekend's schema migration.
Find why the reporting role lost access.

steps.title: Typical causes
steps.body: New table created by a different owner, missing default privileges, revoked PUBLIC, or the role's search_path.

steps.title: Check quickly
steps.body: `\dp app.invoices`, `SELECT current_user;`, `\ddp` (default privileges).

steps.title: Don't
steps.body: Don't grant superuser to 'fix' it.

ticket.short: Reports: permission denied for table invoices
ticket.description: Since Monday our Metabase finance dashboard says 'ERROR: permission denied for table invoices'. Other dashboards work. Please fix urgently, month-end soon!

investigate.label: Check privileges with \dp app.invoices
investigate.reveal: Access privileges: migration_bot=arwdDxt/migration_bot — no entry for orders_ro.

investigate.label: Check who created the table
investigate.reveal: Weekend migration ran as migration_bot, which recreated invoices (DROP + CREATE).

investigate.label: Check \ddp default privileges
investigate.reveal: Defaults exist only FOR ROLE orders_owner, not for migration_bot.

investigate.label: Restart Metabase
investigate.reveal: Same error.

options: Table recreated by migration_bot, so orders_owner's default privileges didn't apply
diagnosis.why: Default privileges are per creating role; objects created by migration_bot got none.

resolution: GRANT SELECT ON app.invoices TO orders_ro
Verify the dashboard loads
Change migrations to run SET ROLE orders_owner (or ALTER TABLE … OWNER TO orders_owner)
Add ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES FOR ROLE migration_bot as a safety net
Add a post-migration grants check in CI

closure.model: Root cause: weekend migration recreated app.invoices as migration_bot; default privileges only existed for orders_owner, so orders_ro lost SELECT. Fix: granted SELECT, changed migrations to SET ROLE orders_owner, added defaults for migration_bot. Verified: finance dashboard loads; \dp shows orders_ro=r.

lessons.title: Lab: Logical backups with pg_dump

scenes.text: A developer drops app.coupons on production.

steps.title: pg_dump formats
steps.body:
- Plain SQL (`-Fp`), restore with psql
- **Custom** (`-Fc`), compressed, selective restore with `pg_restore -t`
- Directory (`-Fd`) with parallel `-j`
`pg_dumpall --globals-only` for roles/tablespaces.

steps.title: Consistency
steps.body: pg_dump takes a consistent snapshot without blocking normal reads/writes.

steps.title: Mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting globals (roles)
- Never testing restores

lessons.title: Lab: Physical backups and point-in-time recovery

scenes.text: Someone ran UPDATE without WHERE at 14:32:10; logical dumps are 12 h old.
Base backup + WAL archive restores to 14:32:00.

steps.title: PITR
steps.body: Take base backups with `pg_basebackup` (or pgBackRest/Barman) and archive WAL continuously (`archive_mode = on`, `archive_command`). To recover: restore the base backup, set `restore_command` and `recovery_target_time`, create `recovery.signal`, start.

steps.title: Settings
steps.body: `recovery_target_time = '2026-11-26 14:32:00+05:30'`, `recovery_target_action = 'promote'`

steps.title: Mistakes
steps.body:
- WAL archive gaps (monitor archiver failures in pg_stat_archiver)
- Recovering over the only copy of the data directory

activity.prompt: Order the PITR steps to recover to just before the bad UPDATE.
items: Stop the application writes and note the bad statement's time (14:32:10)
Provision a recovery server (never overwrite the only copy)
Restore the latest base backup taken before 14:32
Set restore_command to fetch archived WAL
Verify data, then promote and export/repoint as agreed

lessons.title: Lab: Calculate RPO and backup storage

scenes.text: Management asks: how much data could we lose, and how much storage do backups need?
Answer with numbers.

steps.title: RPO and RTO
steps.body: **RPO** = max data loss (time); **RTO** = max time to restore. With WAL archiving every completed 16 MB segment or `archive_timeout = 60s`, RPO ≈ 1 minute.

steps.title: Storage
steps.body: Base 200 GB weekly × 4 retained + WAL 30 GB/day × 28 days = 800 + 840 = 1,640 GB.

steps.title: Mistake
steps.body: Promising zero RPO without synchronous replication.

lessons.title: Lab: Set up streaming replication

Create a hot standby db-pg02 (10.20.0.16) with pg_basebackup.

steps.title: Streaming replication
steps.body: Primary: `wal_level = replica`, `max_wal_senders`, a replication role, pg_hba `host replication replicator 10.20.0.16/32 scram-sha-256`. Standby: `pg_basebackup -R` writes `standby.signal` and `primary_conninfo`.

steps.title: Replication slots
steps.body: Slots stop the primary removing WAL the standby still needs — but an abandoned slot fills the disk. Monitor `pg_replication_slots`.

steps.title: Mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting `-R`
- Running heavy writes on a standby (it's read-only)

lessons.title: Lab: Monitor replication lag

scenes.text: Finance says the replica shows yesterday's orders.

steps.title: Where to look
steps.body: Primary: `pg_stat_replication` (state, sent_lsn, replay_lsn, replay_lag). Standby: `now() - pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp()`. Bytes: `pg_wal_lsn_diff(sent_lsn, replay_lsn)`.

steps.title: Common causes
steps.body: Long queries on the standby with `max_standby_streaming_delay`, slow disks, network, hot_standby_feedback trade-offs.

steps.title: Mistake
steps.body: Measuring time lag on an idle primary (no new transactions looks like 'lag').

scenes.text: db-pg01's disk controller fails; Patroni manages the cluster with etcd.

steps.title: HA stack

steps.title: Planned vs unplanned
steps.body: Use switchover for maintenance; failover only when the leader is gone.

steps.title: Mistake

lessons.title: Lab: Read an EXPLAIN ANALYZE plan

scenes.text: SELECT … WHERE customer_id = 42 takes 3.8 s.

steps.title: Plan nodes
steps.body: Seq Scan, Index Scan, Index Only Scan, Bitmap Heap Scan; joins: Nested Loop, Hash Join, Merge Join. Compare **estimated rows** vs **actual rows**; look for big mismatches and high 'Rows Removed by Filter'.

steps.title: Use BUFFERS
steps.body: `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` shows shared hit/read pages — I/O cost.

steps.title: Careful
steps.body: EXPLAIN ANALYZE executes the query — wrap DML in BEGIN … ROLLBACK.

lessons.title: Lab: Composite indexes and column order

scenes.text: Dashboard: WHERE status = 'PAID' AND created_at > now() - '7 days' ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 50.
One composite index serves both filter and sort.

steps.title: Rules of thumb
steps.body: Equality columns first, then range/sort column: `(status, created_at)`. A B-tree on (a, b) helps `WHERE a = ?` and `WHERE a = ? AND b > ?`, not `WHERE b > ?` alone. Partial indexes (`WHERE status = 'PAID'`) and covering `INCLUDE (total)` reduce size and heap visits.

steps.title: Index
steps.body: `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY ON app.orders (status, created_at DESC) INCLUDE (total);`

steps.title: Mistakes

steps.title: MVCC

Autovacuum triggers when dead tuples > `autovacuum_vacuum_threshold + scale_factor × reltuples` (defaults 50 + 0.2 × rows).

steps.title: Hot tables

steps.title: Wraparound
steps.body: XIDs are 32-bit; old rows must be **frozen**. `age(datfrozenxid)` approaching ~2 billion forces PostgreSQL to stop new XIDs to protect data. Anti-wraparound autovacuum runs at `autovacuum_freeze_max_age` (default 200M).

steps.title: Diagnose
steps.body: `SELECT datname, age(datfrozenxid) FROM pg_database;` then per table `age(relfrozenxid)`; look for long transactions, prepared transactions and stale slots.

steps.title: Never
steps.body: Never kill autovacuum workers that are doing anti-wraparound vacuum.

steps.title: Deadlocks
steps.body: Two transactions each hold a lock the other needs. PostgreSQL detects it after `deadlock_timeout` (1 s) and aborts one. Fix by consistent lock ordering, shorter transactions, or `SELECT … FOR UPDATE` in a fixed order.

steps.title: Log details

steps.title: Not a DB bug

lessons.title: Lab: Design resource URLs

scenes.text: Tara inherits an API with /getOrder, /createOrder and /deleteOrderById. Every new feature adds another verb URL and nobody can guess the next one.
A REST design uses nouns for things and lets the HTTP method carry the action: GET /orders/42, POST /orders, DELETE /orders/42.

steps.title: Resources are nouns
steps.body:
A **resource** is a thing the API exposes: an order, a user, a book. Use **plural nouns** for collections (`/orders`) and the id for one item (`/orders/42`).

Nest only when the child cannot exist without the parent: `/orders/42/items`. Go deeper than two levels and clients suffer; link instead.

steps.title: Verbs to nouns
steps.body:
- `/getOrder?id=42` becomes `GET /orders/42`
- `/createOrder` becomes `POST /orders`
- `/cancelOrder` becomes `POST /orders/42/cancellation` (an action modelled as a sub-resource) or `PATCH /orders/42` with a status field

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using verbs in paths (`/deleteUser`).
- Mixing singular and plural (`/user/1` and `/orders`).
- Putting file extensions or versions of the business logic in the path.
- Using uppercase and underscores: prefer lowercase and hyphens (`/purchase-orders`).

lessons.title: Lab: Pick the right status code

scenes.text: A mobile app always receives 200 OK, even when a login fails; the error is hidden inside the JSON. The team's dashboards show 100% success while users complain.
Accurate status codes let clients, proxies, caches and monitors react without parsing the body.

steps.title: The five families
steps.body:
- **2xx** success: 200 OK, 201 Created (with a `Location` header), 204 No Content.
- **3xx** redirection: 301/302/304 (not modified).
- **4xx** the client erred: 400 bad request, 401 not authenticated, 403 forbidden, 404 not found, 409 conflict, 422 unprocessable, 429 too many requests.
- **5xx** the server erred: 500, 502, 503, 504.

steps.title: A quick map
steps.body:
- Create a record: `201 Created`.
- Read a record that exists: `200`; missing: `404`.
- Delete succeeds with no body: `204`.
- Body is malformed JSON: `400`; valid JSON but breaks a rule: `422` (or 400 by team convention).

steps.title: 401 vs 403
steps.body: **401** means 'I do not know who you are' (missing or bad credentials). **403** means 'I know who you are and you may not do this'. Mixing them confuses clients.

activity.prompt: Write status(method, exists, valid) following the rules: invalid input -> 400; POST -> 201; GET/PUT -> 200 if exists else 404; DELETE -> 204 if exists else 404. Check the printed cases.

    if method == 'POST':
        return 201
    if method == 'DELETE':

print(status('POST', False, False))
print(status('GET', True, True))

lessons.title: Lab: Safe and idempotent methods

scenes.text: A flaky network makes the app retry a request. The customer is charged twice because the retried call was a POST.
Knowing which methods are safe to repeat tells you which calls clients and proxies may retry automatically.

steps.title: Two properties
steps.body:
A method is **safe** if it does not change server state (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS). It is **idempotent** if doing it N times has the same effect as once (GET, HEAD, PUT, DELETE, OPTIONS).

**POST** is neither: two POSTs may create two records. **PATCH** is not idempotent by definition, though a particular patch can be designed to be.

steps.title: PUT versus POST
steps.body: `PUT /users/7` with the full document always leaves user 7 in the same state, however often you send it. `POST /users` creates a new user each time unless you add an idempotency key (later in this pack).

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Treating 'idempotent' as 'returns the same response'. A second DELETE may return 404 instead of 204, yet the server state is the same, so DELETE is still idempotent.

quiz.why: Idempotency is about effect on state, not identical responses.

quiz.q: Which methods may a proxy safely retry automatically?
options: Idempotent ones such as GET and PUT
quiz.why: Retrying idempotent calls cannot double-apply the action.
GET must not change state and repeating it is harmless.

courses.summary: Learn how GraphQL lets clients ask for exactly the fields they need, how resolvers fetch them, and how to avoid the N+1 trap.

lessons.title: Lab: Ask for exactly the fields you need

scenes.text: A REST endpoint /users/1 returns 40 fields. The mobile screen needs two, but all 40 travel over a weak network.
In GraphQL the client names the fields and the response mirrors the query shape.

steps.title: Schema and queries
steps.body:
A GraphQL **schema** is a typed contract: types, fields, and the entry points `Query` and `Mutation`.

A query is a tree of field names. The response JSON has the same tree, containing only the requested fields. There is usually **one endpoint** (`POST /graphql`).

steps.title: A query
steps.body:
```graphql
query { user(id: 1) { name email } }
```
returns `{"data":{"user":{"name":"Asha","email":"asha@example.com"}}}`.

steps.title: Trade-offs
steps.body: GraphQL needs query-cost limits (depth, complexity), has harder HTTP caching than REST, and errors come back with status 200 plus an `errors` array. It is not automatically better; it fits many clients with varied data needs.

activity.prompt: Write pick(obj, fields) returning a new dict with only the keys in fields (ignore missing keys). Print the result for the sample user.

quiz.why: Queries are sent to a single endpoint; the query selects the data.

options: Receiving more fields than the client needs
quiz.why: REST endpoints return fixed shapes, often with unused fields.

quiz.q: A GraphQL query fails validation. A typical HTTP status is:
options: 200 or 400 depending on server, with an errors array in the body
quiz.why: GraphQL reports errors in the body; transport status varies by server and spec version.

scenes.text: A blog screen needs a user, their posts, and each post's title. Maya's executor must walk the query tree and call a resolver for every field.
A resolver is a function that knows how to produce one field's value.

steps.title: Execution
steps.body:
The executor starts at a root field, calls its resolver, then for each sub-selection calls child resolvers on the result. Lists are resolved item by item.

Resolvers can read a database, call another service or compute a value.

steps.title: Nested selection

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Forgetting that a list field returns a list of selected objects, not a single one.

lessons.title: Lab: Find and fix the N+1 problem

scenes.text: The posts page lists 10 posts with their authors. Profiling shows 11 database queries: one for posts, then one per post for the author.
That is the N+1 problem: it hides in naive resolvers and grows with the list size.

steps.title: Why it happens

steps.title: HMAC signatures

An **HMAC** combines a secret key with the message: `HMAC-SHA256(secret, body)`. The sender puts the hex digest in a header. The receiver computes its own digest over the **raw body bytes** and compares.

steps.body: Re-serialising parsed JSON before hashing. Whitespace changes alter the digest; sign and verify the raw bytes.

steps.title: Token bucket
steps.body: A bucket holds up to **capacity** tokens and refills at **rate** tokens per second. Each request takes one token; with no tokens the request is rejected (429). Short bursts are allowed up to the capacity, while the long-run average stays at the refill rate.

    tokens = min(capacity, tokens + (t - last) * rate)
    last = t
    if tokens >= 1:
        tokens -= 1
        return True
    return False

lessons.title: Lab: Offset versus cursor pagination

scenes.text: A feed uses ?page=2. While Rohit scrolls, new posts arrive, so page 2 repeats items from page 1.
Offsets count rows from the start; when rows are inserted, positions shift. Cursors point at a specific item instead.

steps.title: Two styles
steps.body:
**Offset/limit**: `?limit=10&offset=20`. Simple and allows jumping to a page, but the database scans and discards 20 rows, which grows slow for deep offsets, and inserts cause duplicates or gaps.

**Cursor (keyset)**: `?limit=10&after=<last id>`. The query is `WHERE id > :after ORDER BY id LIMIT 10`, which uses the index and stays stable.

steps.title: Response shape
steps.body: `{"items": [...], "next_cursor": "eyJpZCI6MTB9"}` where the cursor is an opaque (often base64) token; clients must not parse it.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Ordering by a non-unique column such as created_at alone. Add the id as a tie-breaker.

items = [{'id': i} for i in range(1, 8)]

def page(items, limit, after=None):
    rest = [x for x in items if after is None or x['id'] > after]
    chunk = rest[:limit]
    nxt = chunk[-1]['id'] if len(rest) > limit else None
    return ([x['id'] for x in chunk], nxt)

print(page(items, 3, 3))
print(page(items, 3, 6))

steps.title: How it works
steps.body:
The client generates a unique key (a UUID) per logical operation and sends `Idempotency-Key: <uuid>`. The server stores `key -> response`. A second request with the same key returns the stored response instead of repeating the work.

Store keys for a limited time (for example 24 hours) and reject the same key with a different body (422/409).

steps.title: Race conditions
steps.body: Two identical requests may arrive at the same moment. Use an atomic insert (unique constraint) so only one proceeds.

steps.title: Which methods?
steps.body: GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent by design. Keys are for POST (and sometimes PATCH).

total = 0

def pay(key, amount):
    global total
    if key in seen:
        return seen[key]
    total += amount
    seen[key] = ('charged', amount)
    return seen[key]

print(pay('k1', 500))
print(pay('k2', 300))
print(total)

**OpenAPI** (formerly Swagger) is a YAML/JSON format describing paths, parameters, request bodies, responses and schemas (JSON Schema vocabulary). Tools generate docs, SDKs, mocks and validators from it.

A schema lists `type`, `required` properties and constraints.

lessons.title: Lab: Breaking or non-breaking?

scenes.text: Three changes shipped together: a new optional field, a renamed field and a stricter validation rule. Two partners broke.
Before releasing, classify every change from the point of view of an existing client.

steps.title: The rule of thumb
steps.body:
**Non-breaking (additive)**: new endpoint, new optional response field, new optional request parameter, new enum value *if clients are told to tolerate unknown values*.

**Breaking**: removing or renaming a field, changing a type, making an optional request field required, tightening validation, changing status codes or meaning.

steps.title: Be liberal in what you read
steps.body: Tell client developers to ignore unknown fields. This makes additive changes safe (the tolerant reader pattern).

steps.title: Versioning options

lessons.title: Lab: Predict the event-loop order

Node runs your synchronous code to completion first, then drains microtasks (promises), then timers.

steps.title: One thread, an event loop
steps.body:
JavaScript runs on one thread. Slow work (network, disk, timers) is handed to the system and its callback is queued. The **event loop** takes callbacks from queues when the call stack is empty.

Order in one turn: 1) all synchronous code; 2) **microtasks** (promise callbacks, `queueMicrotask`); 3) the next **macrotask** such as a `setTimeout` callback.

steps.title: Promise.all

`await a(); await b(); await c();` runs one after another (sum of times). Starting them first and using `await Promise.all([a(), b(), c()])` takes about the **longest** one.

`Promise.all` rejects as soon as one rejects; `Promise.allSettled` waits for all and reports each outcome. Results keep the **input order**, not the completion order.

steps.title: Common mistake

Inside an `async` function, `await` turns a rejection into a thrown exception. Catch it with `try/catch`. Use `finally` for cleanup such as closing connections; it runs whether or not an error occurred.

steps.title: Retry design

steps.title: Queues

A **queue** decouples producers from consumers. The request enqueues a job (`send_email(order=42)`) and responds at once. Workers pull jobs, run them and acknowledge. If a job fails it is retried; after N failures it moves to a **dead-letter queue** for humans to inspect.

Most queues deliver **at least once**, so jobs must be **idempotent**.

steps.title: Tools
steps.body: Redis-backed (Celery, RQ, BullMQ), cloud queues (SQS, Pub/Sub, Service Bus), brokers (RabbitMQ, Kafka).

steps.title: LRU

activity.solution:
from collections import OrderedDict

class LRU:
    def __init__(self, capacity):
        self.cap = capacity
        self.d = OrderedDict()

    def get(self, k):
        if k not in self.d:
            return None
        self.d.move_to_end(k)
        return self.d[k]

    def put(self, k, v):
        self.d[k] = v
        self.d.move_to_end(k)
        if len(self.d) > self.cap:
            self.d.popitem(last=False)

c = LRU(2)
c.put('a', 1)
c.put('b', 2)
c.get('a')
c.put('c', 3)
print(c.get('a'), c.get('b'), c.get('c'))
print(list(c.d))
activity.hint: move_to_end on every access; popitem(last=False) removes the oldest.

scenes.text: Prices changed at noon but the site showed old values until evening, because entries were cached with no expiry.
Cache-aside: read the cache, on a miss read the source and store it with a time to live; invalidate on write.

steps.title: Cache-aside
steps.body:
1. `get(key)` from cache. 2. On miss, load from the database. 3. Store with a **TTL**. 4. On update, **delete** (invalidate) the key so the next read reloads.

TTL bounds staleness even when invalidation is missed. Beware the **cache stampede**: many requests missing the same key at once; mitigate with locks, request coalescing or jittered TTLs.

steps.title: Famous quote
steps.body: There are two hard things in computer science: cache invalidation and naming things. Keep the design simple.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Caching per-user data under a shared key, leaking one user's data to another.

db = {'p1': 100}
cache = {}
db_calls = 0
TTL = 60

def get_price(sku, now):
    global db_calls
    hit = cache.get(sku)
    if hit and hit[1] > now:
        return hit[0]
    db_calls += 1
    v = db[sku]
    cache[sku] = (v, now + TTL)
    return v

print(get_price('p1', 0))
print(get_price('p1', 30))
db['p1'] = 120
print(get_price('p1', 59))
print(get_price('p1', 61))

steps.title: How indexes work
steps.body:
A B-tree index keeps keys sorted, so equality (`=`), ranges (`>`, `BETWEEN`) and `ORDER BY ... LIMIT` on the leading column are fast. Cost: extra disk and slower INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE.

Indexes do **not** help when: you apply a function to the column (`LOWER(email) = ...` unless there is an expression index), the pattern starts with a wildcard (`LIKE '%abc'`), or the column has very few distinct values (a boolean-like status).

steps.title: Composite indexes
steps.body: Order matters: an index on (customer_id, order_date) serves `WHERE customer_id = ?` and `WHERE customer_id = ? ORDER BY order_date`, but not `WHERE order_date = ?` alone.

steps.title: Check with EXPLAIN
steps.body: Always confirm with the database's plan viewer (`EXPLAIN` / `EXPLAIN ANALYZE`) on realistic data.

steps.title: ACID

**Atomicity** all or nothing; **Consistency** constraints hold; **Isolation** concurrent transactions do not see each other's half-finished work; **Durability** committed data survives a crash.

lessons.title: Lab: Base62 short codes

scenes.text: The shortener stores each URL under an auto-increment id. Showing '4815162342' in a link is ugly, so the team converts it to a compact code.
Base62 uses 0-9, a-z, A-Z: 62 symbols per character.

steps.title: Capacity of a code
steps.body:
With 62 symbols, a 7-character code can represent 62^7 = 3,521,614,606,208 distinct values (about 3.5 trillion). That is plenty for 100 million new links per month for several decades.

Encoding: repeatedly divide the number by 62 and map the remainders to symbols (most significant last, so reverse). Decoding multiplies back.

steps.title: Sequential ids leak volume
steps.body: Auto-increment ids reveal how many links exist and are guessable. Mitigate with a random or shuffled id range, or by using random codes checked for uniqueness.

steps.title: Common mistake

lessons.title: Lab: Back-of-envelope capacity

scenes.text: The interviewer says: 100 million new links per month, reads are 100 times writes, keep records for 5 years. Estimate, do not guess.
Estimation turns a vague requirement into numbers that drive design choices.

steps.title: Method
steps.body:
1. Writes per second = monthly writes / (30 x 86,400) = 100,000,000 / 2,592,000 = about 38.6.
2. Reads per second = writes x ratio, about 3,860 on average; plan for peaks of 2-5x.
3. Storage = records x bytes per record: 100 M x 12 months x 5 years = 6 billion records x 500 bytes = 3 TB.
4. Bandwidth = QPS x response size.

Then decide: 3 TB fits a sharded or a large single-node database; 3,860 reads/s is easy with a cache in front. State assumptions aloud and round sensibly.

steps.title: Common mistakes

steps.title: Approach

scenes.text: Each of three services in the checkout path promises 99.9%. The product page promises 99.9% as well. Is that what customers get?
Components in a chain multiply availabilities; redundancy in parallel multiplies failure probabilities.

steps.title: Formulas
steps.body:
- **Series** (all must work): A = A1 x A2 x ... Three services at 99.9% give 0.999^3 = 99.7003%.
- **Parallel** (any one is enough, independent failures): A = 1 - (1 - A1)(1 - A2). Two 99% instances give 1 - 0.01 x 0.01 = 99.99%.
- **Downtime per year** = (1 - A) x 525,600 minutes. 99.9% allows 525.6 minutes (about 8.8 hours); 99.99% about 52.6 minutes.

Independence is an assumption: shared databases, regions and deployments create correlated failures.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Counting two replicas of the same bug, or in the same rack or zone, as independent.

lessons.title: Lab: Fan-out on write or on read?

scenes.text: A news feed stores posts. When a user opens the app, how do we build their feed quickly? The answer changes for ordinary users and for celebrities.

steps.title: Trade-offs

- **Write fan-out (push)**: on post, insert the post id into each follower's feed list (often in a cache). Reads are fast (one list), writes cost followers-many operations.
- **Read fan-out (pull)**: on feed load, fetch recent posts of everyone you follow and merge. Writes are cheap, reads are expensive.
- **Hybrid**: push for ordinary accounts, pull for celebrities, merge at read time.

Decide with numbers: writes x followers versus reads x followees.

steps.title: Numbers
steps.body: A post by a user with 200 followers costs 200 inserts (cheap). A post by someone with 10,000,000 followers costs 10 million inserts: too heavy to push synchronously.

scenes.text: The pull side of the feed has recent posts from several followed accounts, each already sorted newest first. The app needs the top 5 overall.

    [(95, 'b1'), (60, 'b2')],

    out = []

    return out

rounds.q: Explain idempotency in HTTP. Which methods are idempotent and why does it matter for retries?
rounds.model: An operation is idempotent if repeating it has the same effect on server state as doing it once. GET, HEAD, PUT and DELETE are idempotent; GET is also safe because it does not change state. POST is not, so a retried POST may create two orders. Clients, proxies and queues can safely retry idempotent calls automatically. For POST I accept an Idempotency-Key header, store the first result under the key and return it for repeats, using a unique constraint to handle concurrent duplicates.
followups: What if two identical requests arrive at the same instant?
How long do you keep keys?

rounds.q: A customer was charged twice after a network timeout. Walk me through how you would find the cause and prevent it.
rounds.model: First I stop the bleeding: refund the duplicate and check how many customers are affected by querying payments with the same order id within a short window. Then I trace one case with the request id through the logs to see whether the client retried after a timeout and the server processed both. The fix is idempotent payments: a client-generated idempotency key, a unique constraint on key or order, and returning the original result on repeat. I add a reconciliation job and an alert on duplicate charges, and write a test that sends the same request twice.
followups: What if the payment provider itself charged twice?

rounds.q: The /orders endpoint got slower after a release: p95 went from 200 ms to 2 s. How do you investigate?
rounds.model: I check dashboards for what changed and when: deploy markers, traffic, errors. I look at traces to see which span grew, usually a database query or an external call. The slow query log and an EXPLAIN plan reveal a missing index or an N+1 pattern introduced by the release (for example loading items per order in a loop). If customers are hurting I roll back or disable the feature flag first, then fix with a join or batched query or an index, and add a performance test or alert on p95 so it is caught next time.
followups: How would you reproduce it locally?

rounds.q: What is the N+1 query problem and how do you fix it?
rounds.model: N+1 is when code runs one query to fetch a list and then one more query per item, for example orders then each order's customer, producing N+1 round trips. It scales badly with list size. Fixes are a JOIN, a single query with an IN list (batching), eager loading in the ORM, or a DataLoader in GraphQL. I detect it with query counters in tests and tracing.
followups: When is a join worse than two queries?

rounds.q: Authentication versus authorization: what is the difference, and what mistakes do you see with JWTs?
rounds.model: Authentication proves who you are; authorization decides what you may do, including whether this specific object belongs to you. Common JWT mistakes: trusting the algorithm in the header or accepting 'none', not checking exp, aud or issuer, putting secrets in the payload because it is only encoded, and storing tokens where XSS can read them. I verify with a fixed algorithm, keep access tokens short-lived and always check object-level permissions on the server.
followups: How do you revoke a JWT?

rounds.q: How would you cache product pages and keep them fresh when prices change?
rounds.model: I would use cache-aside: read from the cache, on a miss load from the database and store with a TTL. On a price update I invalidate the key, and the TTL bounds staleness if an invalidation is missed. To avoid a stampede on hot keys I use request coalescing or jittered TTLs. I include only shared data in shared keys, never user-specific data, and monitor hit ratio and eviction rate.
followups: What about a CDN in front?

lessons.title: Lab: Mock interview: system design

scenes.text: The interviewer opens a blank board: 'Design a service that shortens links and shows click counts.' The first minute decides the tone.
Follow the structure from the case studies: clarify, estimate, API, data, architecture, deep dive, trade-offs.

steps.title: Reminder
steps.body: Ask about scale and features before drawing. Say your numbers aloud. Choose the simplest design that meets them and name what you would change at 10x scale.

steps.title: Trade-offs
steps.body: Every choice has a cost: say what you gave up.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Listing technologies (Kafka, Redis, Kubernetes) with no reason tied to a requirement.

tips: Name the trade-off of each choice.

rounds.q: Design a URL shortener that also reports click counts.
rounds.model: I would clarify scale (say 100M links a month, reads 100x writes), then estimate about 40 writes/s, 4k reads/s and about 3 TB over five years. API: POST /links returns a short code, GET /{code} redirects with 302 so clicks reach us. Codes come from a counter or ID ranges encoded in base62 (7 characters gives 3.5 trillion values). Reads go through a cache in front of a replicated key-value or SQL store. Click counting is asynchronous: publish a click event to a queue and aggregate, so redirects stay fast. I would add rate limits and malicious URL checks.
followups: How do you avoid hot keys?

rounds.q: How would you rate-limit this public API per customer across many servers?
rounds.model: I would use a token bucket per API key: capacity allows short bursts, refill rate sets the average. Counters live in a shared fast store such as Redis, updated atomically (a Lua script or atomic increment with expiry), or the limit is enforced at the gateway. Over-limit requests receive 429 with a Retry-After header. Limits are per identity, with separate limits for expensive endpoints, and I monitor rejected counts.
followups: What happens if Redis is down?

rounds.q: Design the news feed for a social app with celebrities and ordinary users.
rounds.model: For ordinary users I push new post ids into followers' cached feed lists (fan-out on write), so reads are cheap. For celebrities with millions of followers pushing is too costly, so their posts are pulled and merged at read time. The feed API uses cursor pagination. I skip precomputing feeds for inactive users and rank candidates by relevance. Posts and media are stored separately; media sits behind a CDN.
followups: How do you handle a user unfollowing someone?

rounds.q: Estimate the storage and throughput for a chat app with 50 million messages a day, 200 bytes each, kept for a year.
rounds.model: 50 million a day is about 580 messages per second on average (50e6 / 86,400); with a peak factor of 3-5 plan for about 3,000 per second. Storage is 50e6 x 365 x 200 bytes = about 3.65 TB per year before replication and indexes; with 3 replicas about 11 TB. That fits a sharded store, sharded by conversation id to keep ordering within a conversation cheap.
followups: How would you change this if media was included?

rounds.q: The primary database fails at peak time. What should your design do?
rounds.model: A replicated setup with automatic failover promotes a replica within seconds to minutes; the application reconnects using a managed endpoint and retries idempotent calls. During promotion the service may degrade to read-only. I accept a small window of possible data loss with asynchronous replication or use synchronous replication for critical data. Backups and point-in-time restore are the last line of defence, and failover is rehearsed with game days. Alerts and a runbook make the response routine.

rounds.q: How would you make this service observable in production?
rounds.model: I would expose metrics for request rate, errors and latency percentiles, plus saturation (the golden signals), use structured logs with a correlation id and distributed tracing across services. I define SLOs, for example 99.9% of redirects under 100 ms, and alert on SLO burn and user-visible symptoms rather than every CPU blip. Dashboards per service and runbooks link from alerts.
followups: What would you alert on first?

A 302 redirect for a shortener lets you:
50 million messages per day is about how many per second on average?

options: Bursts up to capacity with a steady average rate

lessons.title: Lab: Mock interview: behavioural and HR

scenes.text: The last conversation is about how Meera works with people: incidents, disagreements, deadlines and growth. Technical skill alone does not decide the offer.
Use STAR: Situation, Task, Action, Result, and finish with what you learned.

steps.title: STAR
steps.body:
**Situation**: one or two sentences of context. **Task**: your responsibility. **Action**: what *you* did (not 'we'). **Result**: a measurable outcome, then **learning**. Prepare 5-6 true stories that can answer many questions: an incident, a conflict, a deadline, a failure, a mentoring moment, a proud project.

Be honest about mistakes. Interviewers value ownership and learning far more than a perfect record.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Blaming others, vague 'we' answers, no result, or inventing a story you cannot discuss in depth.

steps.title: Ask questions
steps.body: Prepare two or three: how success is measured in the first 90 days, how on-call works, how decisions are documented.

rounds.q: Tell me about a production incident you were involved in. What happened and what did you do?
rounds.model: Last year a release made checkout latency spike during a sale (situation). I was on call and owned diagnosis (task). I first rolled back the change to restore service within 12 minutes, then used traces and the slow query log to find an unindexed query introduced in the release (action). We added the index, a latency alert and a pre-release load test; checkout p95 returned to normal and we avoided repeat incidents (result). I learned to separate mitigation from root cause and to write the timeline while it is fresh.

rounds.q: Describe a time you disagreed with a teammate about a technical decision.
rounds.model: A teammate wanted to introduce a message queue for a feature I believed a simple background job could handle. I asked about his concerns, then we listed requirements and compared options on cost, complexity and failure modes, with a quick prototype and numbers for expected load. We chose the simpler job with a clear path to a queue if volume grew. It shipped two weeks sooner, and we documented the decision so it could be revisited.
followups: What if you could not agree?

rounds.q: Tell me about a deadline where quality and speed were in conflict.
rounds.model: A partner demo date moved up by a week. I met the product owner to separate must-haves from nice-to-haves, cut two features, and kept tests and review on the payment path where bugs are costly. I told stakeholders the risks plainly and tracked the shortcuts as tickets. We demoed on time with no critical bugs, and the deferred items were delivered in the next sprint.
followups: How do you track technical debt?

rounds.q: Why do you want this role, and what do you want to learn in the next year?
rounds.model: I want this role because the team builds high-traffic APIs, which matches my experience with backend services and my interest in reliability. In the next year I want to deepen my system design skills, learn more about observability and on-call practice, and take ownership of a service end to end. I believe my testing habits and ability to explain technical trade-offs would help the team from the start.
followups: What kind of manager helps you do your best work?

rounds.q: How do you give and receive code review feedback?
rounds.model: When reviewing I comment on the code, not the person, explain the reason and suggest options, separating blocking issues from preferences. I keep my own pull requests small with context so reviews are quick. When I receive feedback I assume good intent, ask questions when unclear, and thank reviewers; a review once caught a race condition I missed, which taught me to write a concurrency test.
followups: Tell me about feedback that was hard to hear.

rounds.q: What questions do you have for us?
rounds.model: I would ask how success is measured in the first 90 days, what the on-call and incident process looks like, how technical decisions are made and documented, how engineers are mentored, and what the biggest technical challenge for the team is this year.
followups: Which of these matters most to you?

lessons.title: Lab: Red, green, refactor with slugify

story.title: The URL that broke the blog

scenes.text: Titles with symbols produced URLs like /Rock & Roll!!. Dana decides to write the tests first and then the function.
TDD loop: write a failing test (red), make it pass with the simplest code (green), clean up (refactor).

steps.title: The cycle
steps.body:
1. **Red**: write one small test for behaviour that does not exist yet and watch it fail (a test that cannot fail proves nothing).
2. **Green**: write the simplest code that passes.
3. **Refactor**: improve names and structure while the tests stay green.

Repeat in tiny steps. The tests become a safety net and a living specification.

steps.title: A test list
steps.body: slugify('Hello World') -> 'hello-world'; extra spaces and symbols collapse into one hyphen; no leading or trailing hyphen; empty string gives empty string.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Writing all the code first and the tests afterwards: tests then mirror the implementation and miss the requirement.

activity.prompt: Implement slugify(s): lowercase, replace every run of non-alphanumeric characters with a single '-', and strip leading/trailing '-'. The test table runs automatically.

import re

def slugify(s):
    pass

cases = [('Hello World', 'hello-world'), ('  Rock & Roll!! ', 'rock-roll'), ('A--B', 'a-b'), ('', ''), ('Python 3.12', 'python-3-12')]
for given, want in cases:
    got = slugify(given)
    print('PASS' if got == want else 'FAIL', repr(given), '->', repr(got))

tests.expect:
PASS 'Hello World' -> 'hello-world'
PASS '  Rock & Roll!! ' -> 'rock-roll'
PASS 'A--B' -> 'a-b'
PASS '' -> ''
PASS 'Python 3.12' -> 'python-3-12'

activity.hint: re.sub with [^a-z0-9]+ after lower(), then strip('-').

lessons.title: Lab: Boundary values expose the bug

story.title: Everyone with exactly 90 got a B

steps.title: Boundary value analysis

For a rule such as 'A if score >= 90', test 89, 90 and 91. For ranges test the minimum and maximum, plus one outside each. Add the empty input, zero, negative, very large, and `None` where relevant.

**Equivalence classes**: inputs the code treats alike need only one representative each, plus their edges.

steps.body: Off-by-one (`<` vs `<=`), empty collections and null handling cause most real defects.

steps.title: Test doubles

- **Fake**: a light working implementation (in-memory repository).
- **Mock**: also records how it was called so the test can assert on interactions.
- **Spy**: a real object wrapped to record calls.

Common mistake

lessons.title: Lab: Triage tests onto the pyramid

scenes.text: The team's suite is 900 browser tests that take two hours and fail randomly. Releases wait for them.
Most checks should be fast unit tests; fewer integration tests; very few end-to-end journeys.

steps.title: Test levels
steps.body:
- **Unit**: one function/class, no network or DB; milliseconds; thousands of them.
- **Integration**: several parts with a real DB or HTTP; seconds; hundreds.
- **End-to-end (E2E)**: the whole system through the UI; slow and brittle; a handful for critical journeys (login, checkout).

The **pyramid** shape (many, fewer, few) gives fast feedback. An 'ice-cream cone' (mostly E2E) is slow and flaky.

steps.title: Contract tests
steps.body: Between services, contract tests (see the API pack) replace many E2E checks.

lessons.title: Lab: Compute branch coverage

scenes.text: The dashboard says 92% line coverage but a refund bug shipped. The failing branch was never exercised.
Coverage tells you what code ran, not whether the assertions were meaningful.

steps.title: Kinds
steps.body:
**Line coverage**: lines executed. **Branch coverage**: each `if` taken both ways. Branch is stricter: `if x: y()` can reach 100% lines with the false branch never run.

Coverage is a **floor, not a goal**: low coverage proves risk; high coverage proves nothing about assertion quality. Mutation testing (changing code to see if tests fail) measures that.

steps.title: Arithmetic
steps.body: A function with 3 `if` statements has 6 branch outcomes. If tests exercised 4 of them, branch coverage = 4/6 = 66.7%.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Chasing a percentage with assertion-free tests.

activity.prompt: Write branch_cov(total_branches, hit) returning the percentage rounded to 1 decimal, and untested(all_branches, hit) returning the sorted list of branches never hit. Run the sample.

lessons.title: Lab: Cure a flaky test

scenes.text: The checkout test fails one run in ten, and the team clicks 'rerun' until green. Real regressions now hide among the noise.
A flaky test passes and fails on the same code. Find the cause, do not retry blindly.

steps.title: Common causes
steps.body:
- **Time**: sleeps, timeouts, 'now', time zones.
- **Order dependence**: tests share state or a database.
- **Concurrency**: races, async not awaited.
- **External services**: real network calls.
- **Randomness** without a seed.

Fixes: wait for a condition (poll with timeout), isolate data per test, inject fakes, seed randomness, run tests in random order to find coupling.

steps.body: Move a proven flaky test to a quarantine list with an owner and deadline; do not leave it blocking or silently ignored.

steps.title: Collect evidence
steps.body: Record failures with logs, seeds and screenshots before changing anything.

lessons.title: Lab: A reducer for the shopping badge

story.title: The badge that showed the wrong number

scenes.text: The cart icon updates from five components, each calling its own setter. Sometimes they disagree.
A reducer centralises every state change as (state, action) -> new state.

steps.title: Reducer rules
steps.body:
A **reducer** is a pure function: same inputs, same output, no mutation, no side effects (no fetch, no random, no Date.now()). Actions are plain objects such as `{type: 'add', qty: 2}`.

In React: `const [state, dispatch] = useReducer(reducer, initial)`. Calling `dispatch({type:'add', qty:2})` makes React run your reducer and re-render.

steps.title: JSX
steps.body:
```jsx
<button onClick={() => dispatch({ type: 'add', qty: 1 })}>Add</button>
```

lessons.title: Lab: Narrowing a union with typeof

scenes.text: Kiran's shop app accepts a quantity from a form. Sometimes it is the number 3, sometimes the string "3".
On a sale day the cart total printed "13" instead of 4, because a string was concatenated with a number.
A union type string | number forces every use to prove which one it is first. That proof is called narrowing.

steps.title: Unions and narrowing
steps.body:
A **union** type such as `string | number` says a value may be either. The compiler only lets you use members common to both until you **narrow** it with a check.

Checks the compiler understands: `typeof x === "string"`, `Array.isArray(x)`, `x instanceof Date`, `"id" in x`, and equality with `null`.

steps.title: Example
steps.body:
```ts
function len(x: string | number): number {
  if (typeof x === "string") return x.length; // x is string here
  return x;                                   // x is number here
}
```
Inside each branch the type is narrower than outside.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body:
`typeof null` is `"object"`. Check `x === null` explicitly before treating an object as non-null.

Also, `any` switches narrowing off: prefer `unknown`, which forces a check before use.

steps.title: Prefer unknown to any
steps.body: Use `unknown` for data you do not control (JSON, form input). It is the type-safe top type: you must narrow before you can use it.

lessons.title: Lab: Discriminated unions for states

scenes.text: A drawing tool stores circles and rectangles. Each has different fields.
A bug computed a rectangle's area from a missing radius and returned NaN.
Adding a shared literal field, kind, lets the compiler know exactly which fields exist.

steps.title: The pattern
steps.body:
A **discriminated union** is a union of object types that share a literal property (the discriminant).

```ts
type Shape =
  | { kind: "circle"; r: number }
  | { kind: "rect"; w: number; h: number };
```
A `switch (s.kind)` narrows `s` in each case.

steps.title: Exhaustiveness
steps.body: Add a `default` branch that assigns `s` to a variable of type `never`. If someone adds a new kind and forgets a case, the compiler reports an error at that line.

steps.title: Where you see it
steps.body: Redux actions, API results (`{ok:true,data}` vs `{ok:false,error}`), and UI loading states (`idle | loading | success | error`) all use this pattern. It makes impossible states unrepresentable.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Using optional fields (`data?`, `error?`) on one type allows nonsense like both set or neither set. Split into variants instead.

steps.title: Offset vs cursor
steps.body:
**Offset**: `?page=3&size=20` becomes `LIMIT 20 OFFSET (page-1)*size`. Simple, but deep pages are slow and rows shift when data changes.

**Cursor (keyset)**: `?after=<last id>` becomes `WHERE id > :after ORDER BY id LIMIT 20`. Stable and fast with an index.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Page 3, size 20 gives offset (3-1)×20 = 40. Total pages for 95 rows = ceil(95/20) = 5.

steps.title: Common mistake

steps.title: Idempotency-Key
steps.body: The client sends a unique key (such as a UUID) in an `Idempotency-Key` header with the POST. The server stores the key and the result. A repeat with the same key returns the stored result and does nothing new.

steps.title: Implementation notes
steps.body:
- Store key with a request fingerprint
- Same key, different body: reject with 422 or 409
- Expire keys after a window (e.g. 24 hours)
- Make storing the key and creating the charge atomic

steps.title: The three metrics
steps.body:
- **LCP** (Largest Contentful Paint): when the main content appears. Good: **2.5 s or less**; poor: over 4.0 s.
- **INP** (Interaction to Next Paint): how quickly the page responds to taps and clicks. Good: **200 ms or less**; poor: over 500 ms.
- **CLS** (Cumulative Layout Shift): unexpected movement. Good: **0.1 or less**; poor: over 0.25.

Lab data (Lighthouse) is for debugging; **field data** (real users, RUM) decides the rating.

steps.title: Common fixes
steps.body: LCP: optimise the hero image, preload it, reduce server time. INP: break up long JavaScript tasks. CLS: set width/height on images and reserve space for ads.

Cache-Control tells browsers and CDNs how long a response stays fresh and when to revalidate.

steps.title: Key headers
steps.body:
- `Cache-Control: max-age=31536000, immutable`: fresh for a year; use with **fingerprinted filenames** (`app.3f9a1c.js`) so a new build means a new URL.

- `Cache-Control: no-store`: do not keep it (sensitive data).

lessons.title: Lab: Calculate colour contrast

scenes.text: The designer's light grey on white looked elegant on a calibrated monitor. In sunlight on a phone it vanished, and users with low vision could not read it at all.
WCAG defines a contrast ratio formula: 4.5:1 for normal text at level AA.

steps.title: The formula
steps.body:
Relative luminance L = 0.2126 R + 0.7152 G + 0.0722 B, where each channel c (0-1) is first linearised: if c <= 0.03928 then c/12.92 else ((c + 0.055)/1.055)^2.4.

Contrast ratio = (L_lighter + 0.05) / (L_darker + 0.05), from 1:1 to 21:1.

WCAG 2.x AA: **4.5:1** normal text, **3:1** large text (about 18 pt, or 14 pt bold) and UI component boundaries; AAA: 7:1 and 4.5:1.

steps.title: Famous grey
steps.body: #767676 on white is about 4.54:1, the lightest grey that passes AA for body text.

steps.title: Common mistake

def lum(hex_color):
    h = hex_color.lstrip('#')
    chans = [int(h[i:i + 2], 16) / 255 for i in (0, 2, 4)]
    lin = [c / 12.92 if c <= 0.03928 else ((c + 0.055) / 1.055) ** 2.4 for c in chans]
    return 0.2126 * lin[0] + 0.7152 * lin[1] + 0.0722 * lin[2]

def contrast(fg, bg):
    a, b = lum(fg), lum(bg)
    hi, lo = max(a, b), min(a, b)

lessons.title: Lab: Parameterised queries stop SQL injection

scenes.text: A lookup built its SQL by joining strings. A search box value containing quote characters changed the meaning of the query and returned every user.
Injection happens when data is mixed with code. Parameters keep them separate.

steps.title: Why it works
steps.body:
If you build `"... WHERE name = '" + user_input + "'"`, input such as `' OR '1'='1` becomes part of the SQL **syntax**. With a **parameterised query** (`WHERE name = ?` plus a separate values list) the database receives the SQL and the data separately, so the data can never become code.

Defence in depth: least-privilege database accounts, input validation (type, length, allow-list), ORM use correctly (raw string fragments are still dangerous), and no detailed SQL errors shown to users.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Escaping by hand: error-prone.
- Parameterising values but concatenating table or column names from input; use an allow-list for identifiers.
- Believing the front end validation is enough.

steps.title: Why it still matters
steps.body: Injection stays on the OWASP Top 10 list of web risks because string-built queries keep appearing in new code.

Cross-site scripting (XSS) is injection into HTML/JavaScript contexts; the cure is context-aware output encoding.

steps.title: Contexts
steps.body:
Encode for the place the data lands: **HTML text** (`< > &`), **HTML attribute** (also quotes), **JavaScript** and **URL** contexts each need their own encoding. Modern frameworks (React, Angular, Vue) encode text interpolation by default; danger returns with `innerHTML`, `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`, `v-html`, `bypassSecurityTrust...`.

If you must allow rich text, sanitise with a maintained library (such as DOMPurify) using an allow-list of tags. Add **CSP** as a second layer, and set cookies `HttpOnly` so stolen script cannot read the session id.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Blocklisting '<script>' (attackers use other vectors).
- Encoding on input instead of on output: the right encoding depends on the output context.
- Using innerHTML for plain text; use textContent.

steps.title: Result
steps.body: `<script>alert(1)</script>` encoded becomes `<script>alert(1)</script>` and is displayed as text.

lessons.title: Lab: Salted, slow password hashing

story.title: The leaked table of fast hashes

scenes.text: A breached site stored unsalted SHA-256 of passwords. Within hours most were recovered from precomputed tables and fast guessing.
Passwords need a unique salt per user and a deliberately slow, memory- or CPU-hard algorithm.

steps.title: Rules
steps.body:
- Never store plaintext or reversible encryption of passwords.
- Use a password hashing function: **Argon2id** (preferred), **scrypt**, **bcrypt**, or **PBKDF2** with a high iteration count (OWASP's guidance for PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 is in the hundreds of thousands of iterations; check the current cheat sheet).
- A random **salt** per password defeats precomputed tables and hides equal passwords.
- Compare in constant time. Keep the algorithm parameters with the hash so you can upgrade later.
- Enforce length (long passphrases) and check against known-breached lists; offer MFA.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Plain SHA-256/MD5.
- One global salt ('pepper' kept in code is not a per-user salt).
- Truncating passwords silently.

steps.title: Lab note
steps.body: The lab uses 1,000 iterations so it runs instantly in the browser. Production values must be far higher.

lessons.title: Lab: Verify a signed token properly

scenes.text: A library accepted tokens whose header said alg: none, so anyone could forge a login. Verification must pin the algorithm.
A JWT is three base64url parts: header, payload, signature. Check the signature, the algorithm you expect and the expiry.

steps.title: Checks
steps.body:
1. Split into three parts. 2. **Require the expected algorithm** (for example HS256) instead of trusting the header. 3. Recompute the HMAC over `header.payload` with your secret and compare in constant time. 4. Only then trust the claims: `exp` (expiry), `nbf`, `iss` (issuer), `aud` (audience), `sub` (subject).

The payload is **encoded, not encrypted**: never put secrets in it. Prefer short-lived access tokens, store refresh tokens carefully and revoke on logout or compromise.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Accepting 'none' or switching algorithm family based on the header.
- Ignoring exp or aud.
- Keeping tokens in localStorage where XSS can read them; HttpOnly cookies are safer for browsers.

steps.body:

- hosts: web

    - name: Install nginx

    - name: Deploy config

    - name: reload nginx
